title: How does a foreign company close its branch or liaison office in India?
seo_title: Closing a Foreign Company's Branch/Liaison Office India
meta_description: Closing a branch or liaison office in India runs through your AD Category-I bank, not the RBI, and needs tax and MCA clearances first. Here is the order.
format: step-by-step process with timelines and fees where official
intro: A foreign company winding down its branch office or liaison office in India cannot simply stop operating and walk away. The office was set up with the Reserve Bank of India's permission under the foreign exchange rules, and closing it needs a formal application, tax clearance and a round of approvals before the parent company can lawfully take its remaining funds out of the country. Since February 2010, this process is handled by the company's own designated Authorised Dealer Category-I bank rather than by the RBI's regional office directly, which surprises foreign parents used to dealing with the RBI on the way in.

The sequence matters more than any single document. Get the order wrong, typically by trying to remit funds or deregister before the tax authority has cleared the office, and the file stalls with the bank for months while missing clearances are chased down one by one.

sections.heading: Why an AD bank, not the RBI, handles the closure
paragraphs: Branch offices, liaison offices and project offices of foreign entities are established in India under the Master Direction the RBI issues on this subject. Historically, the RBI's own central office or regional office handled closure applications, with the central office dealing with branch offices and the regional office with liaison offices. Since 1 February 2010, that function has moved to the designated AD Category-I bank the office has been operating through, which now reviews the closure file and reports the completed closure back to the RBI rather than the RBI processing it first-hand.

This matters practically because the AD bank applies its own internal checklist on top of the RBI's requirements, and different banks are not always equally fast or consistent about what they will accept. A foreign parent should contact its AD bank early, well before it intends to actually shut the office, rather than treating the bank as a last step after everything else is arranged.

sections.heading: Clearances to line up before applying
paragraphs: The income tax clearance is usually the slowest piece and should be started first. The office needs a no-objection or tax clearance certificate from the jurisdictional income tax authority confirming that all tax dues, including any outstanding demands, have been settled, because the AD bank will not release the final remittance without it. Any pending assessment, even an old one the office considered closed informally, can hold up this certificate, so it is worth checking for open notices well in advance rather than discovering one at the closure stage.

In parallel, the office needs a no-objection certificate from the Registrar of Companies confirming there is no objection to it closing its registered place of business in India, since a foreign company's branch or liaison office is itself registered with the Registrar under the Companies Act's provisions for foreign companies. The parent company typically also has to confirm, in a letter to the AD bank, that no legal proceedings are pending against the office in any Indian court and that there is no legal impediment to the proposed remittance of the closing balance.

sections.heading: The remittance and reporting steps
paragraphs: Once the tax clearance, the Registrar's no-objection and the parent company's confirmations are in hand, the AD bank reviews the complete closure application and, if satisfied, permits the outward remittance of the office's remaining balance to the parent company abroad. The remittance itself can be routed through any AD Category-I bank, but it needs a no-objection certificate from the specific AD bank that was designated for the office's operations, so the designated bank stays in the loop even if a different bank handles the actual transfer.

After the remittance is completed, the AD bank reports the closure to the RBI, which is what formally ends the office's recognised existence from the foreign exchange regulator's point of view. The office's bank accounts in India are closed as part of this sequence, and any assets that cannot simply be remitted as cash, such as office equipment or a leased premises, need to be disposed of or the lease terminated separately before the file can be closed out.

sections.heading: What commonly delays a closure
paragraphs: The single biggest delay is starting the tax clearance process too late. Foreign parents sometimes decide to shut an office quickly, for cost or strategic reasons, and only then discover that the tax clearance alone can take a meaningful stretch of time if the local tax officer wants to review several years of filings before signing off. Starting that conversation with the tax department as soon as the closure decision is made, rather than after the AD bank has been approached, avoids the office sitting half-closed with ongoing compliance obligations for months longer than necessary.

A second common delay is treating the Registrar's no-objection as a formality. If the office's annual filings with the Registrar are not current, or if there are unresolved compliance notices, the Registrar can withhold the no-objection until those are cleared, which pushes the whole closure timeline back. A third is forgetting that employees of the office need to be settled, including final dues and any required notices, before the office can genuinely be said to have ceased operations, since an unresolved employment claim can surface as exactly the kind of pending proceeding the parent company's confirmation letter is meant to rule out.

sections.heading: How this differs from winding up an Indian subsidiary
paragraphs: Foreign groups sometimes treat closing a branch or liaison office as interchangeable with striking off or winding up an Indian subsidiary company, and the two are governed by entirely different frameworks. A subsidiary is an Indian company incorporated under the Companies Act, and closing it runs through either the fast-track removal of name process with the Registrar or a formal winding-up procedure, neither of which involves an AD bank unless the company also happens to hold foreign investment that needs separate reporting on the way out.

A branch, liaison or project office, by contrast, was never a separate Indian legal entity. It is an extension of the foreign parent, permitted to operate here under the foreign exchange rules, and that is exactly why its closure runs through the AD bank and the RBI's framework rather than through the company winding-up machinery. A group that has both structures in India, perhaps a liaison office that preceded a later subsidiary, needs to run two separate closure exercises if it is exiting both, and treating the subsidiary's closure checklist as covering the office, or the reverse, is a frequent and avoidable source of missed steps.

faqs.q: Does the foreign parent apply to the RBI directly to close an Indian branch office?
faqs.a: No. Since 1 February 2010, this work is handled by the office's designated AD Category-I bank, which reviews the closure application against the RBI's requirements and later reports the completed closure to the RBI. The parent applies to the bank, not to the RBI's regional or central office.

faqs.q: What is the single most important clearance to start first when closing a branch or liaison office?
faqs.a: The income tax no-objection or clearance certificate, since it is usually the slowest to obtain and the AD bank will not release the closing remittance without it. Any unresolved assessment or notice should be sorted out well before the formal closure application goes to the bank.

faqs.q: Can the office's closing funds be remitted through any bank, or only the bank it has operated with?
faqs.a: The actual remittance can go through any AD Category-I bank, but that bank needs a no-objection certificate from the office's originally designated AD bank first. In practice, most offices simply remit through the same bank that has handled their account throughout.

faqs.q: What happens to the Registrar of Companies registration when a branch office closes?
faqs.a: The office needs a no-objection certificate from the Registrar before the AD bank will complete the closure, confirming there is no objection to the office ceasing its registered place of business in India. Outstanding annual filings or compliance notices with the Registrar can delay this certificate.

references: Reserve Bank of India, Master Direction on Establishment of Branch Office, Liaison Office or Project Office in India by Foreign Entities
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, and regulations on establishment of a place of business by a person resident outside India
Companies Act, 2013, provisions applicable to foreign companies registered with the Registrar of Companies
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: foreign company. TARGET QUERY: how does a foreign company close its branch or liaison office in India. DEMAND EVIDENCE: no direct search-trend evidence was seen; this topic was chosen because it is a natural and distinct follow-on question to the firm's existing guide on setting up a branch, liaison or project office, which the search results themselves treat as a standard closing step for the same structures; no search volume is stated. AD Category-I bank handling closure since 1 February 2010, rather than the RBI directly: confirmed from the RBI's own master circular text as quoted in search results and corroborated by a second, independent practitioner source (vjmglobal.com) describing the same handover of function. Need for income tax no-objection/clearance certificate before remittance, and that outstanding tax dues should be cleared first: confirmed from two independent sources (website.rbi.org.in liaison/branch/project office page and carajput.com), which both listed this as a precondition. Registrar of Companies no-objection requirement: reported by one practitioner source (carajput.com); treated here as a standard, uncontested procedural step consistent with a foreign branch/liaison office's registration obligations under the Companies Act's provisions for foreign companies, rather than as a disputed point, since no source contradicted it, though a second independent confirmation specific to this exact NOC was not separately located in this run. Parent company's no-pending-litigation and no-legal-impediment confirmation letter, and the requirement that the office route its NOC-backed remittance through the designated AD bank even if a different AD bank executes the transfer: confirmed from the RBI source material directly. A 2025 draft FEMA regulation mentioned in one source (KPMG) was not relied on anywhere in this draft because its final/notified status could not be confirmed from a second source in this run.
